diagnosis: Ketosis-prone (Flatbush) type 2 diabetes mellitus presenting in diabetic ketoacidosis, precipitated by a urinary tract infection

examinerBank.question: Walk me through your differential diagnosis for this man's presentation, and how you would rank them.
examinerBank.modelAnswer: Top of the list is ketosis-prone (Flatbush) type 2 diabetes presenting in DKA — obese, African, older-onset, family history of typical type 2 diabetes, with a clear infective precipitant. New-onset type 1 diabetes is next — DKA and weight loss fit, but the obesity and age argue against it, and this needs to be confirmed or excluded with antibodies/C-peptide rather than assumed. Stress hyperglycaemia with ketosis secondary to the UTI in an undiagnosed type 2 diabetic is possible but the degree of acidosis is more than typically seen. HHS is against given significant ketoacidosis and preserved mental state. Secondary diabetes is unlikely given no steroid use or endocrinopathy features.
examinerBank.gradingNotes: Wants a ranked list with reasoning FOR and AGAINST each, not just naming diagnoses. Full marks require explicitly flagging that ketosis-prone type 2 should be considered before committing to type 1.

examinerBank.question: Explain the pathophysiology of why he developed diabetic ketoacidosis despite this most likely being type 2, not type 1, diabetes.
examinerBank.modelAnswer: In ketosis-prone (Flatbush) type 2 diabetes, severe glucotoxicity and lipotoxicity — often precipitated by an acute stressor like infection — transiently 'stun' beta-cell function, producing a temporary but severe relative or absolute insulin deficiency. This is sufficient to unleash unrestrained lipolysis and hepatic ketogenesis, producing DKA indistinguishable biochemically from type 1 DKA. Because the underlying lesion is functional beta-cell stunning rather than autoimmune destruction, beta-cell mass and function typically recover once the glucotoxic insult resolves — which is why these patients are antibody-negative, retain measurable C-peptide, and can often become insulin-independent again.
examinerBank.gradingNotes: Wants the mechanism (glucotoxicity/lipotoxicity → beta-cell stunning → transient insulinopenia → ketogenesis, with expected recovery), not just a restatement of 'he has DKA'.

examinerBank.question: His HbA1c comes back at 11.8%. Given everything else, how much weight do you place on this single result for diagnosing diabetes, and what caveats apply in this population?
examinerBank.modelAnswer: In this case it's not being used as the sole diagnostic criterion because he is acutely symptomatic with confirmed hyperglycaemia and DKA — the confirmation rule (needing two abnormal results in an asymptomatic patient) doesn't apply here. But generally in KZN, HbA1c can be unreliable due to anaemia, HIV, CKD and haemoglobinopathies, all of which are common locally — where HbA1c and glucose disagree, the glucose result should be believed. Here it's used descriptively (reflecting weeks-months of preceding hyperglycaemia) rather than as the diagnostic test itself.
examinerBank.gradingNotes: Tests understanding of the confirmation rule and the specific HbA1c caveats emphasised in the KB — anaemia, HIV, CKD, haemoglobinopathy — and the instruction to trust glucose over HbA1c when they disagree.

examinerBank.question: Once he has recovered from this DKA episode, how would you decide whether he needs to stay on insulin long-term?
examinerBank.modelAnswer: Given his antibody-negative status and preserved C-peptide, this fits ketosis-prone type 2 diabetes, where beta-cell function often recovers after the acute glucotoxic insult resolves. I would continue basal-bolus insulin through the initial recovery period, then, once he is metabolically stable off IV insulin (typically 6-8 weeks later), attempt a structured trial of tapering insulin while introducing metformin, monitoring glucose closely, rather than assuming he needs lifelong insulin as would be the default in true type 1 diabetes.
examinerBank.gradingNotes: Wants explicit mention of the trial-of-withdrawal approach and the time frame/rationale, not just 'continue insulin.'

framework: hyperglycaemic crisis presentation → confirm DKA biochemically → exclude/treat precipitant → classify diabetes type clinically (and with antibodies/C-peptide if unclear) → screen complications and comorbidity → individualise management

patient.name: Bongani Mthembu
patient.occupation: security guard at a shopping centre in Pinetown
patient.personality: stoic, downplays how unwell he feels, worried about losing his job if admitted
patient.openingLine: Doctor, I've been vomiting and my stomach is sore since yesterday... I thought it was something I ate.

presentingComplaint: 2 days of vomiting and abdominal pain with 2 weeks of excessive thirst and urination, now breathing fast

history.fact: Two days ago started vomiting repeatedly and developed constant central abdominal pain; for about 2 weeks before that he had been drinking water constantly and getting up to urinate several times a night
Passing large volumes of urine, day and night, for about 2 weeks — up to 4-5 times overnight
Extremely thirsty, drinking far more water than usual, sometimes 3-4 litres a day
Noticed his work trousers are loose; thinks he has lost about 4kg over the past month
His appetite has actually increased over the past couple of weeks — eating more but still losing weight — though today he has no appetite at all because of the nausea
Family noticed he has been breathing fast and deeply since this morning, and his breath smells 'sweet' or like fruit
Vision has been slightly blurry for the past week, especially reading small print at work
Has never been told he has diabetes before and has never had his sugar checked
His father has 'sugar' diabetes, diagnosed in his 50s, on tablets; no known family history of diabetes diagnosed in childhood or young adulthood
Had burning when passing urine and lower back discomfort for about 5 days before this, which he ignored
Takes no regular medication — no steroids, no antipsychotics, no traditional muti recently
No known drug allergies and no history of reactions to any medicines or foods
Drinks beer socially on weekends, about 4-6 beers on a Saturday, no alcohol during the week; no history of binge drinking or withdrawal
Tested HIV negative about a year ago at a workplace wellness day; not currently on any HIV treatment
No cough, no night sweats, no known TB contacts
Lives in Umlazi with his wife and two children; smokes about 5 cigarettes a day for 10 years; works long night shifts as a security guard with irregular meal times
No chest pain, no leg swelling, no numbness or tingling in his feet, no foot wounds, no erectile difficulties reported so far

examination.general: Obese, visibly dehydrated man, breathing rapidly and deeply (Kussmaul pattern); sweet/acetone smell on breath; dry mucous membranes, reduced skin turgor; acanthosis nigricans noted at the back of the neck; no lipodystrophy, no thrush, no lymphadenopathy
examination.respiratory: Deep, sighing (Kussmaul) breathing; chest clear on auscultation, no crackles or wheeze
examination.cardio: Tachycardic, normal heart sounds, no murmurs; postural BP drop of 20 mmHg systolic on sitting up; JVP not raised
examination.abdo: Diffuse mild tenderness on palpation, soft, no guarding or rebound (pseudo-peritonism of DKA); bowel sounds present; no organomegaly; mild suprapubic and left flank tenderness
examination.neuro: Alert and orientated (GCS 15), no focal deficits; grossly intact sensation on brief screening; reflexes present

other.feet: No ulcers, calluses or deformity; pulses palpable bilaterally; monofilament sensation intact today
other.fundoscopy: Not yet performed — deferred until acutely unwell period settles

investigations.name: Venous blood gas
investigations.result: pH 7.18, HCO3 9 mmol/L, base excess -16, pCO2 3.1 kPa (compensatory)

investigations.name: Urine dipstick
investigations.result: Glucose 4+, ketones 3+, leucocytes 2+, nitrites positive, no haematuria

investigations.name: Mid-stream urine culture
investigations.result: E. coli >10^5 CFU/mL, sensitive to standard agents — confirms UTI as DKA precipitant

investigations.name: U&E and creatinine
investigations.result: Na 132 mmol/L, K 5.6 mmol/L (pre-treatment), urea 9.8 mmol/L, creatinine 118 µmol/L, eGFR 68 mL/min/1.73m²

investigations.name: Full blood count
investigations.result: WCC 14.2 x10^9/L (mild leukocytosis, likely stress/infection), Hb 13.1 g/dL, platelets normal

investigations.name: HbA1c
investigations.result: 11.8% (undiagnosed, poorly controlled hyperglycaemia over preceding weeks-months)

investigations.name: C-peptide (paired with glucose, drawn once acutely stable)
investigations.result: 0.9 nmol/L — preserved, not in the undetectable/type 1 range

investigations.name: Chest X-ray / TB symptom screen
investigations.result: No TB symptoms on screen; CXR clear, no cavitation or infiltrate

investigations.name: Fasting lipogram and urine ACR
investigations.result: Deferred until acute illness resolves, to be done at follow-up once euglycaemic

differentials.dx: Ketosis-prone (Flatbush) type 2 diabetes presenting in DKA
for: family history of typical type 2 diabetes

differentials.dx: New-onset type 1 diabetes presenting in DKA
DKA precipitated by an infective illness in undiagnosed type 2 diabetes (without ketosis-prone phenotype)
for: hyperglycaemia and ketosis can occur in stressed type 2 diabetes
against: degree of ketoacidosis is more marked than typically seen in straightforward stress hyperglycaemia
significant ketosis and acidosis present, which is atypical for HHS
patient alert with GCS 15, not the altered mental state typical of HHS
no features of Cushing's or acromegaly
no history of pancreatitis or alcohol excess pattern

pathophys.polyuria: Glucose exceeds the renal tubular reabsorption threshold (~10-11 mmol/L), causing osmotic diuresis as unreabsorbed glucose drags water into the tubular lumen
pathophys.polydipsia: Osmotic diuresis causes intracellular and extracellular dehydration, raising plasma osmolality and stimulating hypothalamic thirst centres
pathophys.weight loss with increased appetite: Cellular glucose starvation (impaired uptake despite hyperglycaemia) drives catabolism of fat and muscle for energy despite increased calorie intake — a relative insulinopenic state
pathophys.vomiting and abdominal pain: Ketoacidosis directly irritates the gastric mucosa and slows gastric emptying; metabolic acidosis and electrolyte derangement stimulate the vomiting centre — this 'pseudo-peritonism' can mimic a surgical abdomen
pathophys.Kussmaul breathing: Compensatory hyperventilation to blow off CO2 and raise pH in response to severe metabolic (ketoacidotic) acidosis
pathophys.fruity/acetone breath: Volatile ketone body (acetone) exhaled via the lungs
pathophys.blurred vision: Acute osmotic shifts alter the water content and refractive index of the lens, causing transient blurring independent of true retinopathy
pathophys.ketosis-prone type 2 (Flatbush) mechanis: Severe glucotoxicity/lipotoxicity transiently 'stuns' beta-cells, precipitating a temporary absolute insulin deficiency sufficient to trigger DKA; because the underlying defect is beta-cell dysfunction rather than autoimmune destruction, beta-cell function characteristically recovers once glucotoxicity resolves, allowing eventual insulin independence — hence antibody-negative and C-peptide-preserved

staging: Diabetic ketoacidosis, moderate-to-severe (pH 7.18, HCO3 9 mmol/L, significant ketosis); newly diagnosed diabetes, phenotype consistent with ketosis-prone (Flatbush) type 2 diabetes pending recovery-phase reassessment

immediate: Resuscitate with IV 0.9% sodium chloride per DKA protocol (rapid initial bolus then rate guided by hydration status/response)
Start a fixed-rate IV insulin infusion (0.1 units/kg/hour), only after ensuring K+ is not already dangerously low
Monitor and replace potassium aggressively once insulin started (K+ will fall as it shifts intracellularly) — add potassium to fluids once K+ <5.5 mmol/L and urine output confirmed
Hourly capillary glucose, 1-2 hourly ketones/VBG until acidosis resolving
Add 10% dextrose infusion alongside saline once glucose falls below ~14 mmol/L to prevent hypoglycaemia while continuing insulin to clear ketones
Treat the precipitant: empirical antibiotics for the urinary tract infection per local antibiogram, adjust once culture/sensitivity available
VTE prophylaxis once stable; strict fluid balance and hourly observations
definitive: Transition to subcutaneous basal-bolus insulin once eating, drinking and ketones cleared (overlap IV and SC insulin by 1-2 hours)

Given obesity, antibody-negative status and preserved C-peptide, plan a structured trial of insulin reduction/withdrawal with introduction of metformin (± other oral agents) 6-8 weeks after recovery, once glucotoxicity has resolved and beta-cell function has had a chance to recover
Do NOT commit him to a label of lifelong type 1 diabetes on the basis of presenting in DKA alone — reassess type in the recovery phase
Structured diabetes education, home glucose/ketone monitoring, and sick-day rules for future illness
supportive: Dietary counselling and weight management given obesity and metabolic syndrome features
Screen and address cardiovascular risk factors (BP, lipids) once stable
Psychosocial support and reassurance regarding return to work
followUp: Repeat GAD65/IA-2 antibodies and C-peptide are not usually needed again if already clearly negative/preserved, but reassess insulin requirement at 6-8 weeks
Baseline dilated fundoscopy, urine ACR, foot risk screening and fasting lipogram once acutely stable, then annually
HbA1c recheck at 3 months to guide ongoing therapy
Diabetes and TB cross-screening at every future visit given local epidemiology

stationChecklist.item: Characterises the presentation: distinguishes classic osmotic symptoms, tempo of onset, and recognises presentation via a decompensated crisis (DKA) rather than incidental finding
stationChecklist.answer: 2 weeks of polyuria/polydipsia/weight loss with increased appetite, now 2 days of vomiting, abdominal pain and fast breathing
stationChecklist.why: First step of the framework — establishes this is a crisis presentation requiring urgent biochemical confirmation

stationChecklist.item: Actively screens for ketosis symptoms: nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, rapid/deep breathing, breath odour
stationChecklist.answer: All present — vomiting, abdo pain, Kussmaul breathing, fruity breath noted by family
stationChecklist.why: Identifies red flags for DKA requiring urgent management, not just a hyperglycaemia workup

stationChecklist.item: Actively searches for a precipitant (infection symptoms, medication non-adherence, new-onset presentation, drug history)
stationChecklist.answer: 5 days of dysuria and loin discomfort suggestive of urinary tract infection; no steroid/antipsychotic use
stationChecklist.why: DKA always needs an identified and treated precipitant, per the framework's 'exclude acute precipitant' step

stationChecklist.item: Gathers features to classify diabetes type clinically: age, BMI/habitus, tempo, ketosis, family history
stationChecklist.answer: 34 years old, obese (BMI 31), African, father with typical type 2 diabetes, 2-week tempo
stationChecklist.why: Clinical classification comes before reaching for antibodies/C-peptide

stationChecklist.item: Explicitly avoids labelling an obese African patient presenting in DKA as lifelong type 1 diabetes without further testing
stationChecklist.answer: Recognises ketosis-prone (Flatbush) type 2 diabetes as a genuine and locally common possibility requiring active exclusion
stationChecklist.why: Named red flag in the KB — committing to lifelong insulin prematurely is a common and clinically significant error

stationChecklist.item: Requests GAD65/IA-2 autoantibodies and C-peptide (with paired glucose) to resolve diabetes type once the acute crisis is controlled
stationChecklist.answer: Antibodies negative, C-peptide 0.9 nmol/L (preserved) — supports ketosis-prone type 2, not type 1
stationChecklist.why: Framework step 5 — use antibodies/C-peptide only when the answer changes management, exactly the scenario here

stationChecklist.item: Orders and interprets the biochemical confirmation of DKA: glucose, ketones/VBG, U&E (especially potassium)
stationChecklist.answer: Glucose 28.4, pH 7.18, HCO3 9, ketones 5.8 mmol/L, K+ 5.6 pre-treatment
stationChecklist.why: Confirms diagnosis and severity, and guides safe initiation of insulin/fluids/potassium replacement

stationChecklist.item: Performs bidirectional HIV and TB screening as part of new diabetes workup
stationChecklist.answer: HIV negative (tested a year prior), no TB symptoms
stationChecklist.why: Mandatory bidirectional TB-DM and HIV screening per SA/KZN guidelines for every new diabetic

stationChecklist.item: Screens for complications appropriate to a new diagnosis: acanthosis nigricans, postural BP, feet, plans fundoscopy
stationChecklist.answer: Acanthosis nigricans present, postural drop of 20 mmHg, feet currently normal, fundoscopy deferred to when stable
stationChecklist.why: Complication screening is part of the framework even at first presentation of type 2-pattern diabetes

stationChecklist.item: Outlines immediate DKA management: fluids, fixed-rate insulin infusion, potassium monitoring/replacement, treating the precipitant
stationChecklist.answer: IV 0.9% saline, insulin infusion 0.1 U/kg/hr, K+ replacement once <5.5, antibiotics for UTI
stationChecklist.why: Core DKA protocol per SA Adult Hospital Level STGs

stationChecklist.item: Plans definitive management including a structured trial of insulin withdrawal/introduction of metformin once recovered, rather than committing to lifelong insulin
stationChecklist.answer: Transition to SC insulin at recovery, reassess at 6-8 weeks with a trial of oral therapy given antibody-negative, C-peptide-preserved status
stationChecklist.why: Directly reflects the ketosis-prone type 2 management pathway emphasised in the KB
